title: Living the Awakened Life : Reflections on the Dhammapada
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the first chapter of the Dhammapada in Gil Fronsdal's translation, then returns to its opening verses and comments on four themes. Nomon sets the verse "all experience is preceded by mind" beside a psychology study in which subjects recall a red car on an on-ramp that was never in the picture. Nomon then turns to the call to live ethically, to the verse that hatred never ends through hatred, and to the advice to focus on the unpleasant. A Tricycle interview with Bhante Piyananda, Miranda Shaw, Reggie Ray, and Sojun Mel Weitsman supplies different views on pleasure, and Mel's story of Suzuki Roshi taking one drink of champagne at a party closes that thread.

sentences.text: And practice group, which is now Red Cedar Zen.
And he is our guiding teacher and spiritual director.
Thank you very much, Tim, for giving the talk today.
So fun.
Thanks. [unclear: "In here for I roll along and Dharma world"].
I just wanted to update you, and Desiree or John might have something to add, about the beginnings, the seed of an effort towards our future: the campaign.
I guess "campaign" is just the word to use, but it's kind of a military word, so maybe we could have thought of a better one.
But anyway, the campaign towards the future.

You should have seen an email about an online survey, with some open-ended reflection questions about the future of the [unclear: "song"] and a lot of orientation on how we can serve the greater Bellingham community, serve the world.
If you didn't see that, search your email or go to Red Cedar Zen dot org slash campaign.
"Campaign" is the keyword there.
Also, I hope you have marked on your calendar Saturday, March 27th.
We have our annual meeting every year to reflect on where we're at, and this one's extra big and extra annual and extra reflective.
We'll also have the fundraising campaign consultant, Thomas Brunner, who has been supporting us, as well as the usual board report stuff and so on.
So please participate as best you can.
One of the things I really appreciate about the process he's supporting us in so far is this strong effort to take a step back, be really open about it, be really curious.

We know it's going to be a Zen practice group, that's not changing, but what is the deeper meaning of the offering, and how does that eventually manifest as a new physical home and the programs we do and so on and so forth?
So anyway, I want to mention that.
The bottom line of that whole little ramble: please do the survey.
It may take a little bit of time because it's a thoughtful thing, but it's really helpful.
All right, well, I know that we've been exploring on these Sunday talks lately some ideas about awakening or enlightenment as the orientation of the practice, what's the point of it all.

I continue to appreciate that this is all happening, and especially how we're taking such great advantage in this particular program of the zooming world and having speakers from our friends to the north and to the south.

I know Susan LB from Vancouver came, and Jeff Bickner from California, and [unclear: "every day then"] came, each teacher and friend bringing a different piece of the conversation and encouraging us to practice and consider and muse together.
I often have a mindfulness work thing on the weekend, so I miss some of them, but it just makes me so happy to know that they're rolling right along.
I feel grateful to Chris and everybody for that emergence and continuity of practice.
It's really wonderful, so I'll just say thank you.
Every time I manage to show up, and I'm trying to shift some of the things from Sunday to Saturday as I go along, but some of them are all weekend.
Anyway, I thought today I'd bring us into conversation with some of the early Buddhist teachings, which we touch on from time to time.
Our tradition emerged a little bit later, and of course in a way our tradition emerged in the twentieth century, because we're doing our own American version of all this.
But it's worth reflecting back on what a long history it is.
Buddhism first emerged in northern India sometime in the fourth or fifth centuries BCE and eventually spread over about a third of the planet.

It's kind of an amazing thing, going north into China and Tibet and south into Sri Lanka, and then it jumped across the ocean to Southeast Asia: Burma, Thailand, Indonesia, which was a huge Buddhist country back then.
And then from China it filtered its way down and around to Korea, Japan and Vietnam, in the form then of Zen.
We say "Buddhism" like it's one thing, but the more I think about it, Buddhism is really a plural tradition.
I suppose Christianity is really the same: different branches and different schools, so different, with common roots, I think in a common feeling, but some significant differences.
Even though we have an orientation from our version of their version of the Zen, it's good to honor and be curious about all the traditions as we have time and can find reliable sources.
While we were sitting I was remembering a dream I had early this morning that somehow seems relevant.
I was in a kind of overgrown garden in front of this big wooden gate.
It was really old, and I could tell it hadn't been opened in a long, long time, maybe centuries.
But I somehow knew for sure that it could be opened, and when it was opened it would just swing smoothly open.
I don't know if it has something to do with the Dharma talk or something else going on in my subconscious.
So with all that in mind, let's listen a little to a famous teaching from early Buddhism.
This is a Buddhist teaching poem called the Dhammapada, which gets quoted a lot.
I've heard it quoted for decades, but I never really read it.
So I read it.
I got hold of a fairly recent translation by Gil Fransdal.
Here's what the book looks like.
I read the whole thing: it's twenty-six chapters and four hundred and something verses.
Gil is a reliable source.
He also has one foot in our tradition.
He started out in Soto Zen, and I first met him when I was just getting started with Zen at Green Gulch Farm.

Later he realized his true calling was more in the Theravada [unclear: "of Apostani"] insight stream of things, which is like Jack Kornfield and Sharon Salzberg and all those well-known people who adapted the early Buddhism that had carried on in Burma and Thailand and brought it over to America in the seventies, with some simplification of the ritual parts of it.
So Gil knows both sides of that particular fence, and he also went on to get a PhD in Buddhist studies at Stanford, so he's a pretty bright character too.
Anyway, I want to read the first chapter, twenty-something verses, without interrupting myself, and then go back and return to some of them with a few comments, and then have a conversation.
Is my voice okay?
Is it pretty clear?
Oh, good.
I know it's hard to take in a lot of text just orally, and all the more so if the Zoom is distorted.
Okay, chapter one, which Gil called "Dichotomies":
*All experience is preceded by mind, led by mind, made by mind.
Speak or act with a corrupted mind, and suffering follows as the wagon wheel follows the hoof of the ox.*
*All experience is preceded by mind, led by mind, made by mind.
Speak or act with a peaceful mind, and happiness follows*
Like a never-departing shadow.
*"He abused me, attacked me, defeated me, robbed me."
Those who carry on like this, for those carrying on like this, hatred does not end.
"She abused me, attacked me, defeated me, robbed me."
For those not carrying on like this, hatred ends.*
We'll come back to that.
*Hatred never ends through hatred; by non-hate alone does it end.
This is an ancient truth.

Many do not realize that we here must die; for those who realize this,* [unclear: "quarrels and"] *whoever lives focused on the pleasant, senses unguarded and immoderate with food, lazy and sluggish, they will be overpowered by Mara as a weak tree is bent in the wind.
Whoever lives focused on the unpleasant, senses guarded, moderate with food, faithful and diligent, they will not be overpowered by Mara as a stone mountain is unmoved by the wind.*
*Whoever is defiled and devoid of self-control and truth, who wears the saffron robe, is unworthy of the saffron robe.
Whoever has purged the defilements, is self-controlled, truthful and well-established in virtue, is worthy of the saffron robe.
Those who consider the inessential to be essential and see the essential as inessential don't reach the essential, living in the field of wrong intention.
Those who know the essential to be essential and the inessential as inessential reach the essential, living in the field of right intention.*
*As rain penetrates an ill-thatched house, so lust penetrates an uncultivated mind.
As rain does not penetrate a well-thatched house, so lust does not penetrate a well-cultivated mind.
One who does evil grieves in this life, grieves in the next, grieves in both worlds.
Seeing one's own defiled acts brings grief and affliction.
One who makes merit rejoices in this life, rejoices in the next, rejoices in both worlds.
Seeing one's own pure acts brings joy and delight.*
*One who does evil is tormented in this life, tormented in the next, is tormented in both worlds.
Here is tormented, knowing "I have done evil."
Reborn in realms of woe is tormented all the more. [unclear: "when it makes merit"] is delighted in this life, delighted in the next, delighted in both worlds.
Here she is delighted, knowing "I have made merit."
Reborn in rounds of bliss she delights all the more.
One who recites many teachings but, being negligent, doesn't act accordingly, like a cow herd counting others' cows, does not attain the benefits of the contemplative life.

One who recites but a few teachings yet lives according to the Dharma, abandoning passion, ill will and delusion, aware and with mind well freed, not clinging in this life or the next, attains the benefits of the contemplative life.*
So that's all that I know.
It's just the beginning of the poem, which goes on for quite a while, and Gil called that chapter "Dichotomies" because all of those were this or that, this or that, this or that, lots of choices.
The opening verses, which I think are kind of the most famous verses, get quoted a lot.
I'll start out that way.
Let's go back to that.
Gil's translation is:
*All experience is preceded by mind, led by mind, made by mind.
Speak or act with a corrupted mind, and suffering follows as a wagon wheel follows the hoof of an ox.*
That's the one half.
The second half:
*All experience is preceded by mind, led by mind, made by mind.
Speak or act with a peaceful mind, and happiness follows like a never-departing shadow.*
So, corrupted mind versus peaceful mind.
Suffering follows as a wagon wheel follows the hoof of an ox, or happiness follows like a never-departing shadow.
I want to especially focus on the first half of that, because that's pretty interesting.
Gil's translation is "all experience is preceded by mind, led by mind, made by mind."
"Preceded" is interesting because it says the mind came first, right before anything else.
But the word "preceded" doesn't imply the causality exactly.
Did the mind make what happened next, or what you think happened next, or was it just that the mind was there first?
Here's a more traditional, or more usual, translation, I guess, as I understand it from somebody else, I forget the name of this monk.
This translation is:
*All mental phenomena have mind as their forerunner; they have mind as their chief; they are mind-made.*
So all phenomena are mind-made.
I'm excited because on Wednesday I set myself the assignment to explore together with everybody a little bit of neuroscience that seems to be saying a pretty similar thing.
The mind is doing a lot.

We have some assumptions, right, that we're sort of neutral observers of reality, maybe a little biased by our tendencies, but basically we're seeing what we see and we're hearing over here, and we know that's how it is, that's how the world is.
These teachings, and also some of this neuroscience, seem to be saying, "Well, that might not be true."
And how would you know, because you're in the middle of it?
The neuroscientists, in a study, say that the brain seems to generate a lot of stuff that looks like what we're seeing and sounds like what we're hearing.
It is being generated by the brain, actually, as an anticipation of what the brain thinks, based on history mostly, we need right now.
And Buddhism seems to be saying the same thing: the mind seems to be generating our reality.
This is powerful.
This is really a fundamental and powerful thing.
We have expressions like "I saw it with my own eyes," right, as if that gives definitive proof of what happened because I saw it and I remember it.
And "saw," right, in the past tense, is already a bit of a problem.

As before, you know, there are lots of stories of witnesses after crimes and disasters, people who are at the same place at the same time who saw things very differently, with very different stories later.

Occasionally I do enjoy geeking out on psychology, and I've read about psychology experiments where they can experimentally show that our memories and perceptions are very easily switched up and don't always connect so directly with what we're seeing, hearing and so on.
What I remember is that the subjects were shown a series of pictures of cars on the road.
It's a common thing we're looking at, right?
To stay safe, we're driving along looking at cars on the road, so we need to have an accurate idea of what's going on so we don't crash.

The one little tidbit I remember is that they took half of the group, and after they finished looking at these pictures of cars on the road, they asked half of the group, "What color was the car on the on-ramp?"
A majority of subjects did answer with a color.
I think most of them said red, but actually there was no car on the on-ramp in the picture.
The other half they asked, "Was there a car on the on-ramp?" and they mostly answered, "No, there was no car on the on-ramp."
So we could kind of write something like that off, like, "Oh yeah, suggestion."
But the interesting thing is when they interviewed the people further, and it wasn't like the people who saw the red car were saying, "Yeah, I think there was probably a car there."
No, they had a visual memory of a red car sitting there.
Some of them could give fair details about what the red car looked like, what model it was, and so on.
There's no car.
So are we always so sure that what we're seeing, hearing, thinking and assuming is true?

The practice point in the poem, though, is that there may be some differences in mind: although mind is generating reality, some kinds of mind lead more to suffering and some kinds of mind lead more to peace.
In this translation they use the dichotomy of corrupted minds and peaceful minds.
That brings up some interesting questions.
How do we practice having a peaceful mind, where the reality our mind makes will lead more to peace?
And is that peace for us, or peace for everyone?
It is amazing how easily our minds are whipped around, and how we don't even know it.
Here's another example, actually from this morning's New York Times.
I was glancing online and I saw a column about the proposals to increase the national minimum wage, which I keep forgetting how low it is: seven dollars and fifteen cents.
Can you imagine trying to live on that?
Anyway, the columnist was pro raising the minimum wage, and he said a lot of the arguments against it are really resistant to evidence that what they're saying is factually wrong.
He quoted a senator saying something that was wrong.
Then he quoted another science study, which was interesting too, about bias.
So maybe it's a corrupted mind that's biased.

The columnist wrote that Dan Kahan, a professor of law and psychology at Yale [unclear: "not a second a law on psychology"], has found that people's ability to solve math problems collapses when the right answer contradicts their political beliefs.
In a 2013 study Mr.
Khan gave people some data, sometimes describing it as being about the effectiveness of skin cream, something neutral, and sometimes about the effectiveness of gun control.
He gave the subjects very similar math problems to solve using that data, either about skin cream or about gun control effectiveness.
And guess what: the gun control people got the problems wrong a lot more often.
We can't even think straight or add when we don't agree with something.
So are all of our minds corrupted, and is that why we need to practice?
That's one of the first points the poem brings up, and it seems to carry right through to the modern day: our reality is generated by mind, so we have a lot to do to work with our mind.
Whatever this more peaceful mind is, it leads to happiness for self and hopefully for others.
A second theme has to do with the importance of morality, of our ethics, and this too I think is carried through quite well.
Here are the third and fourth verses of that chapter that we heard:
*One who does evil grieves in this life, grieves in the next, grieves in both worlds.
Seeing one's own defiled acts brings grief and affliction.
One who makes merit rejoices in this life, rejoices in the next, rejoices in both worlds.
Seeing one's own pure acts brings joy and delight.*
It goes a little deeper, and this thing comes up a lot.
So here's another verse in the chapter:
*One who makes merit is delighted in this life, delighted in the next, is delighted in both worlds.
Here she is delighted, knowing "I've made merit," and is reborn in realms of bliss, where she delights all the more.*
So it's really good to make merit: you're happier in this life and the next, reborn in realms of bliss.
But this verse and the first one are in a powerful relationship, right?
How do we know?
How do we know if we're doing good, or doing evil, or making merit?
There's the obvious stuff at the extremes that we could all think of.
How about the more middle stuff?
Is this helpful or not helpful?
Should I respond in this way or that way?
Should I live my life this way or that way?
Should I make this choice or that choice?
Should I buy this or not buy this?
We make so many choices all the time, right?
We know from cause and effect, which is deep in early Buddhism, that every choice trickles out throughout the universe and has a huge effect.
So here we have a great, clear pointer to live consciously and live well, but the challenge is how we know.
In future chapters there are some more pointers, but it never gets very specific.
There's no list of precepts or particular rules to follow.

Of course the early monastics had hundreds of rules, which evolved over the course of the community living together, people having problems and the Buddha making rules, but the teachings themselves don't really spell it out.
Here's a verse in the fifth chapter about this question of good and bad:
*No deed is good that one regrets having done, that results in weeping and a tear-streaked face.
A deed is good that one doesn't regret having done, that results in joy and delight.*
So it sounds like there's a role here for reflection.
We make a choice in a moment, and then we reflect: do I regret that?
Maybe later we start to notice our distorted minds have misunderstood the situation.
There was no car on the on-ramp, I was wrong.
What I thought about his or her intentions was wrong.
Or I did something regretful, and I should weep and have a tear-stained face.
Or the reverse: to really reflect.
I think here's where we do have this bias.
We're pretty prone to being worried that we screwed up, right?
But also, when reflecting, if it was a good deed, a deed well done, I should feel joy and delight.
So maybe there's something here about practice over time.
Even though we know the mind is distorting reality, or generating reality in ways we don't always see, we should reflect.
Then in chapter 6 it makes another point.

I'm saying "it" — and "they" — because although this was supposedly written by the Buddha in the tradition, it's pretty clear from the textual evidence that it was a kind of monologue of Buddhist teachings that evolved over hundreds of years.
Some of the verses are definitely straight from suttas, early Buddhist texts that say the Buddha said this.
Whether he did or not is another talk, but some of them clearly came from other speakers.
So it's a monologue of early Buddhist teachings, and I'm not saying the Buddha said this and that necessarily.
But that's okay.
The Buddha said everything, actually, in the end.
Just look on Facebook: the Buddha said a lot of good things.
But anyway, we have the caution to do good, to make merit and not do evil.
We have encouragement to reflect on our actions and see if there's regret.
And then in chapter 6 we have encouragement to get somebody else's input.
This is really good, like *Someone pointing to treasure is the wise person who sees your faults and points them out.
Associate with such a sage.
Good will come of it, not bad, if you associate with one such as this.*
So this is a little bit of a challenging suggestion.
Any teachers in the Sangha, we also need them to point out our faults.
We don't always like that, right?
So this is good, challenging medicine for us.
I didn't have time to go through the whole thing again really carefully, but I didn't see anywhere to associate with people who point out how good you are.
It seems like in our modern psychology we need that too, or we think we do.
So, as a second theme: do good, avoid evil.
Here's a third connected thing that showed up right in the beginning of the text, and it's a little challenging, or a lot challenging.
The way it's written is a little hard to understand orally.
The first part is quotations, like you're saying this, and the second part is a commentary on why you're saying this.
So it's a quote:
*He abused me, attacked me, defeated me, robbed me.*
So it's like I'm saying that, and then the text, or the Buddha, says, *for those carrying on like this, hatred does not end.* And then the contrast:
*She abused me, attacked me, defeated me, robbed me.
For those not carrying on like this, hatred ends.*
And then it says:
*Hatred never ends through hatred.
By non-hate alone does it end.
This is an ancient truth.*
It's also often reversed, I've seen many times.
So if someone abuses you, don't get mad, don't meet that with hatred.
And it's interesting, the way it's expressed here, it's even kind of reinforcing the view that someone abused you.
This seems to be saying that's a bad idea.
This is pretty challenging, right?
What about justice?
What about injustice?
What about boundaries?
What about clear communication?
What about harm happening to other beings?
We're Bodhisattvas, so we want to prevent harm from happening, and yet there's some suggestion here to not meet harmful action with something harmful, or something that's pushing back.
And again, it doesn't really give a lot of details on how to act.

Centuries later there's a whole stream of Indian Buddhism that goes even further and really talks a lot about an extreme kind of patience, really loving and embracing and appreciating people who do you harm, because they're teaching you about your mind.
So maybe it's circling back to that very first pair of verses: is your mind corrupted, or is your mind peaceful when something bad happens to you?
And can you develop a peaceful mind that's so accepting that you're unruffled by somebody harming you, in a way that leads to liberation, that leads to more freedom, that leads to awakening?
I hope you noticed Chris has volunteered to do another study group, so generous, [unclear: "clear time"], Chris, on Shanti Deva.
There's a whole chapter of Shanti Deva's famous text, Bodhi Satva Charyavatara, on and on about this.
It's treasure, those who have abused you, they're your deep teachers.
You're so fortunate, thank goodness, lucky, good for you.
And nothing about pushing back or straightening out or setting boundaries or clarifying, no straightening anybody out.
So this is a challenging teaching.
Of course, it also goes right back to the first one: are we so sure that there was abuse here?
Sometimes it seems really obvious, sometimes it's more subtle, and a lot more than the physical, right?
The psychological is so subtle and powerful.
Actually, the neuroscience book we're gonna look at talks about how, when children aren't given love and support, their brains really don't develop, right?
And their brains don't even regulate the growth of their body.
So mind and matter are not separate, for sure.
Modern science and ancient Buddhism agree there.
So how do we meet that kind of teaching, to just be non-reactive and peaceful in the face of abuse?
Shouldn't we do something?
Shouldn't we respond?
The Dhammapada's next verse in that section does make one suggestion about perspective, a really broad perspective.
It says:
*Many do not realize that we here must die.
For those who realize that, quarrels...*
And really realizing how temporary being alive is, we have no reason to fight with anybody.
We can realize that.
And maybe one way to look at all this, and I kind of bring this out as an open question, is that we always want everything to be tidy in our minds.
We want definitely Buddhism to be right, because we're all pretty invested in Buddhism, right?
I mean, [unclear: "nice of all the forms of Buddhas"] more helpful and wise and deep.
Maybe this part's a little bit off, that's possible.
Or maybe there's a both-and way to practice with it.

Maybe when something harmful and difficult happens, there's both an opportunity to learn about our reactivity, our corruptedness, our confusion, our own hatred and anger and conditioned life, right here's an opportunity to learn about that, and to do something wholesome and helpful.
Right, to not throw out either one.
To feel empathy and compassion with someone who does something really horrible, like mass shooters come to mind.
Wow, that person is acting out of something.
Not to write them off as just a bad person, or rioters at the Capitol, a more recent example, or a messed up person.

Here's another human being, maybe they have something to teach me about my own mind, and to do something, right, as best we can, [unclear: "not going to make"] the world a little safer, healthier, happier place.
What's wise action in response?
I think to jump right to push back, boundaries, fix it, solve it, maybe we miss a really important opportunity.
And there's a reason why these Buddhist sages brought this up so extremely, in this extreme way: don't ever meet that with anything but acceptance and love.

But there's something we can learn when we're really pressed, when we're upset, [unclear: "when we run over"], and maybe that's one of the few ways we can learn something about the stickiness of our mind, something about what the first verse called the corruption in our mind, even though maybe we don't like that word, corruption.
So that's the third theme here.
Live a moral life, but oh, it's the second theme, sorry.
Let me set the third theme, right.
So we have the Understanding the mind creates our experience.
The theme of living a moral life, somehow figuring that out: how can I live a moral life?
And a third theme: can I practice meeting the evils of others with non-evil?
So we can work with all this.
I think here's a fourth theme, which is also kind of confusing, that's deep in early Buddhism especially, and this theme seemed to really evolve through the different Buddhisms.
Here are two verses in our first chapter again, and it's about how we relate to pleasure, to the pleasant and the unpleasant.
So it's another pair of verses, and one seems to be the right course and one seems to be the wrong course.
The wrong course first.
*Whoever lives focused on the pleasant becomes unguarded, immoderate with food*, sorry, I messed up.
*Whoever lives focused on the pleasant* [unclear: "senses"] *unguarded* [unclear: "and moderate"] *with food, lazy and sluggish, will be overpowered by Mara as a weak tree is bent in the wind.
Whoever lives focused on the unpleasant* [unclear: "senses"] *guarded, moderate with food, faithful and diligent, will not be overpowered by Mara as a stone mountain is unmoved by the wind.*
So some of that's really easy to agree with.
The bad case was to be unguarded, [unclear: "in moderate"], lazy and sluggish, and the good case was to be guarded, which is interesting, but moderate, faithful and diligent.
That all sounds good.
But the really interesting point in there, which shows up again and again in early Buddhism, is the pleasant and the unpleasant.
The recommended-against case was to focus on the pleasant, and the recommended case was to focus on the unpleasant: live a life focused on the unpleasant.
So it sounds a little bit like pleasure is a bad thing.
And there's lots of stuff in early Buddhism about guarding the senses, closing the sense gates, not letting things in.
It sounds, to us I think, or to me anyway, kind of reactive and maybe a little fearful.
But also maybe in a way [unclear: "come control come with"] the right word, humble.
Maybe very humble, to recognize that we easily are overwhelmed by desire.
It shifts us off, [unclear: "chance"], yanks us around, causes us to waste time and make bad choices, right?
And we can think about the more powerful desires like sexuality, and that shows up later in the chapter.
I mean, we think of the grass hut, you know, the lust falls in through the poorly created grass hut like the rain, soaks you and messes you up.
So we can kind of nuance this in various ways for sure.
One way to look at it is that the Buddha and these teachers who put this together were talking to monastics.
There was a choice of a certain style of practice there in early Buddhism, where the Buddha apparently felt the way to really awaken is to live a very prescribed and simple lifestyle as a monastic.
That's kind of the only way he taught, apart from some teaching to lay people and so on, but the vast focus was on monastics.
And we're not monastics, so we have to translate a little bit.

In a way we can appreciate and practice with the monastic teachings through some of our rituals, like the ritual of sesshin, which is a version of being a monastic, or being at the monastery for a practice period.
It's kind of like being a temporary monastic.
I think we've all seen how helpful that is, to lose a lot of the stuff you like to do.
If you more or less like doing Zen, I would think so, or you wouldn't be there.
But our preferences get added: things don't happen at the times we necessarily want.
You know, I don't want to hear the wake-up bell at this time of morning, I wanted that for lunch and I got this instead, and so on.
I think it's all in a way sort of privileged and playing around, but still our preferences can get powerfully activated.
We can learn a lot about clinging and a lot about desire.
We notice in sesshin that if we just try to get pleasure, it doesn't work out.
And yet in sesshin I think we all do feel a lot of pleasure, a lot of joy, a lot of delight.
Maybe sometimes it's associated with a sense experience, like the unbelievable sunsets at Samish or something.
But I don't know that we set out, for seven days or our practice lives, to focus on the unpleasant.
So that's pretty interesting.
Why are the early Buddhists focusing in that way?
I mean, we do have strong teachings around not ignoring the unpleasant, right?
Being open to it when it's here.
We say, study your suffering, because we learn a lot from when we're reactive.
And then think back to the previous one, about dealing with it when people are mean to us: we learn a lot from that.
There's something that sounds self-denying here, or life-denying, I think, to our ears.
So I have some curiosity about how to work with that. [unclear: "I'm not curious about us"] about this for ages, and I kind of tend to avoid the topic.
You know, I like this part of this early sutra, I'll just kind of skip that part, which we tend to do.
One way that people talk about it, which I think is a little bit sort of reading in, is that, well, Buddhism is all about the middle way.
And the story of the Buddha, the most common story: he was this insane ascetic, right, so that's too far, pleasure-denying.
Then he realized that wasn't working anymore, after six years of starving himself almost to death.
He accepted the rice porridge from [unclear: "Sudana"], [unclear: "home and go"] from the village, and then awakening happens.
